nameStory: Bird cherry gets its name because birds absolutely love its small, dark cherries, often stripping the tree bare before the fruit fully ripens. The scientific name 'Prunus padus' comes from the ancient Latin name for this tree, with 'padus' referring to the Po River region in Italy where it was well known to Roman botanists.
description: Bird cherry is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that can grow up to 50 feet tall, though it's usually much smaller in New England. It belongs to the rose family and produces distinctive drooping clusters of small white flowers in late spring, followed by small black cherries. Unlike our native cherries, this European species has a more open, spreading growth habit and smooth, dark bark with prominent horizontal lines called lenticels.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers hang in long, drooping clusters (racemes) 3-6 inches long, like white bottle brushes. Each flower has 5 petals and smells sweetly fragrant, blooming after the leaves emerge in late spring.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves are 2-4 inches long with finely serrated edges and a smooth, slightly glossy surface. They're arranged alternately on branches and have a fresh, slightly bitter smell when crushed.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small black cherries about 1/4 inch across hang in clusters, turning from green to red to shiny black. They taste very bitter and astringent, puckering your mouth immediately.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, dark gray to brownish bark marked with distinctive horizontal lines (lenticels) that look like dashes or short stripes. The bark feels relatively smooth compared to our native cherries.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a small tree or large multi-stemmed shrub with an open, somewhat irregular crown. Branches tend to be more spreading than upright, creating a broader silhouette.

habitat: Bird cherry is rarely found in the wild in New England, appearing occasionally as an escaped ornamental near old homesites, parks, or cemeteries. When it does naturalize, it prefers moist, well-drained soils in partially shaded areas along woodland edges or in disturbed sites. With only 7 recorded observations in New England, it's much more likely to be encountered as a planted specimen than a wild tree.

seasonality.spring: Drooping white flower clusters appear in late May after leaves have emerged, creating a distinctive bottlebrush effect that's quite different from native cherries. The sweet fragrance is noticeable from several feet away.
seasonality.summer: Small green cherries develop in hanging clusters, gradually turning red then black by midsummer. Leaves remain dark green and glossy throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to orange-yellow before dropping, and any remaining fruits become shiny black. Birds often strip the fruit before it's fully ripe.
seasonality.winter: Smooth, dark bark with horizontal lenticels is most visible, along with the open branching pattern. Winter buds are small and pointed, arranged alternately on twigs.

funFact: Bird cherry contains compounds that can actually intoxicate birds when they eat large quantities of the fermented fruit, sometimes causing them to fly erratically or become temporarily unable to fly at all - nature's version of a wine tasting gone wrong!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with chokecherry, but bird cherry's flowers hang in longer, more drooping clusters and appear after the leaves emerge, while chokecherry flowers appear with or before the leaves in more upright clusters. Remember: bird cherry's flowers 'droop like a bird's tail feathers.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'hackberry,' bird cherry is completely unrelated to true hackberries (Celtis species), which are in the elm family. This naming confusion exists because both trees produce small, dark fruits that birds enjoy, showing how common names can be misleading across different plant families.
compareHints: Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves. Its smooth bark with horizontal lines also differs from the more furrowed or peeling bark of black cherry and the gray, smooth bark of chokecherry. The bitter, astringent fruit is smaller and more intensely puckering than either chokecherry or black cherry.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
